topic: Ohm's law, power, series and parallel (T5C, T5D)

notes.front: What does Ohm's law say?
notes.back: Voltage equals current times resistance: E = I × R. Rearranged, I = E / R and R = E / I.
notes.explanation: E is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms; knowing any two gives the third.
notes.example: A 10-ohm resistor carrying 2 amperes has 20 volts across it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D01, T5D02, T5D03, T5D12

image.alt: Ohm’s law triangle: E (voltage) on top, I (current) and R (resistance) below. Cover the quantity you want: I = E / R, E = I × R, R = E / I. Beside it, the power formula P = I × E.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D01–T5D03 and T5C08

notes.front: What formula gives electrical power in a DC circuit?
notes.back: P = I × E: power in watts equals current in amperes times voltage in volts.
notes.explanation: It is how you size a power supply or work out what a radio draws; rearranged, I = P / E.

notes.front: What is special about a series circuit?
notes.back: The current is always the same through all its components.
notes.explanation: This one property is what the pool asks about series circuits.
notes.example: Like cars in single file on a one-lane road: every car passes every point, just as the same current passes through every component.

notes.front: What is special about a parallel circuit?
notes.back: The voltage is always the same across all its components.
notes.explanation: It is the mirror image of series, where the current is the same.
notes.example: Unlike series, where every component carries the same current, in parallel each component has the same voltage across it, like appliances plugged into the same supply.

notes.front: In the formulas for Ohm’s law and power, what do E, I, R and P stand for?
notes.back: E is voltage, I is current, R is resistance, P is power.
notes.explanation: The pool writes the formulas with these letters, so you must know them to pick the right one.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D01, T5D02, T5D03, T5C08

notes.front: To find current, divide voltage by resistance: {{c1::I = E / R}}.
notes.explanation: More voltage pushes more current; more resistance lets less through.

notes.front: To find voltage, multiply current by resistance: {{c1::E = I × R}}.
notes.explanation: This is Ohm’s law in its basic form.

notes.front: To find resistance, divide voltage by current: {{c1::R = E / I}}.
notes.explanation: Multiplying E × I instead gives power, not resistance.

notes.front: Electrical power in a DC circuit is {{c1::P = I × E}}.
notes.explanation: Current times voltage: 12 volts at 2.5 amperes gives 30 watts.

notes.front: How do you find the current needed to deliver a given power at a given voltage?
notes.back: Divide power by voltage: I = P / E.
notes.explanation: It is the power formula rearranged: 120 watts at 12 volts needs 10 amperes.

notes.front: What formula is used to calculate electrical power (P) in a DC circuit?
notes.choices:
A) P = I x E
B) P = E / I
C) P = I² x E
D) P = I / E
notes.choicesExplained: B: E / I gives resistance, not power. C: there is no squared term in this formula. D: I / E divides where the power formula multiplies (P = I × E).
notes.explanation: Power is current times voltage, so the two are multiplied: 10 A at 13.8 V gives 138 W. Dividing voltage by current gives resistance instead.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C08, T5C09, T5D03

notes.front: How much power is delivered by a voltage of 13.8 volts DC and a current of 10 amperes?
notes.choices:
A) 138 watts
B) 0.7 watts
C) 23.8 watts
D) 3.8 watts
notes.choicesExplained: B: 0.7 comes from dividing current by voltage. C: 23.8 is the sum; power is the product. D: 3.8 is the difference; power is the product.

notes.front: How much power is delivered by a voltage of 12 volts DC and a current of 2.5 amperes?
notes.choices:
A) 4.8 watts
B) 30 watts
C) 14.5 watts
D) 0.208 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 4.8 is voltage divided by current. C: 14.5 is the sum; power is the product. D: 0.208 is current divided by voltage.

notes.front: How much current is required to deliver 120 watts at a voltage of 12 volts DC?
notes.choices:
A) 0.1 amperes
B) 10 amperes
C) 12 amperes
D) 132 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 0.1 is voltage divided by power, upside down. C: 12 is the voltage, not the current. D: 132 is the sum of power and voltage.

notes.front: What formula is used to calculate current in a circuit?
notes.choices:
A) I = E x R
B) I = E / R
C) I = E² x R
D) I = E² / R
notes.choicesExplained: A: E × R does not give current. C: there is no squared term in Ohm’s law. D: there is no squared term in Ohm’s law.
notes.explanation: Divide both sides of E = I × R by R to get I = E / R: more voltage drives more current, and more resistance lets less through.

notes.front: What formula is used to calculate voltage in a circuit?
notes.choices:
A) E = I x R
B) E = I / R
C) E = I² x R
D) E = I² / R
notes.choicesExplained: B: I / R does not give voltage. C: there is no squared term in Ohm’s law. D: there is no squared term in Ohm’s law.
notes.explanation: E = I × R is Ohm's law in its basic form; the formulas for current and resistance come from rearranging it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D02, T5D01, T5D03

notes.front: What formula is used to calculate resistance in a circuit?
notes.choices:
A) R = E x I
B) R = E / I
C) R = E + I
D) R = E - I
notes.choicesExplained: A: E × I gives power, not resistance. C: adding E and I means nothing electrically. D: subtracting I from E means nothing electrically.
notes.explanation: Divide both sides of E = I × R by I to get R = E / I. Multiplying E × I would give power instead.

notes.front: What is the resistance of a circuit in which a current of 3 amperes flows when connected to 90 volts?
notes.choices:
A) 3 ohms
B) 30 ohms
C) 1/30 ohm
D) 270 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: A: 3 is the current, not the resistance. C: 1/30 is current divided by voltage, upside down. D: 270 is voltage times current.
notes.explanation: R = E / I = 90 V / 3 A = 30 ohms.

notes.front: What is the resistance of a circuit for which the applied voltage is 12 volts and the current flow is 1.5 amperes?
notes.choices:
A) 18 ohms
B) 0.125 ohms
C) 8 ohms
D) 13.5 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: A: 18 is voltage times current. B: 0.125 is current divided by voltage, upside down. D: 13.5 is the sum.
notes.explanation: R = E / I = 12 V / 1.5 A = 8 ohms.

notes.front: What is the resistance of a circuit that draws 4 amperes from a 12-volt source?
notes.choices:
A) 3 ohms
B) 16 ohms
C) 48 ohms
D) 8 ohms
notes.choicesExplained: B: 16 is the sum. C: 48 is voltage times current. D: 8 is the difference.
notes.explanation: R = E / I = 12 V / 4 A = 3 ohms.

notes.front: What is the current in a circuit with an applied voltage of 120 volts and a resistance of 80 ohms?
notes.choices:
A) 9600 amperes
B) 200 amperes
C) 0.667 amperes
D) 1.5 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 9600 is voltage times resistance. B: 200 is the sum. C: 0.667 is resistance divided by voltage, upside down.

notes.front: What is the current through a 100-ohm resistor connected across 200 volts?
notes.choices:
A) 20,000 amperes
B) 0.5 amperes
C) 2 amperes
D) 100 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 20,000 is voltage times resistance. B: 0.5 is resistance divided by voltage, upside down. D: 100 is the difference.
notes.explanation: I = E / R = 200 V / 100 ohms = 2 A.

notes.front: What is the current through a 24-ohm resistor connected across 240 volts?
notes.choices:
A) 2400 amperes
B) 0.1 amperes
C) 10 amperes
D) 5760 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 2400 does not follow from I = E / R. B: 0.1 is resistance divided by voltage, upside down. D: 5760 is voltage times resistance.
notes.explanation: I = E / R = 240 V / 24 ohms = 10 A.

notes.front: What is the voltage across a 2-ohm resistor if a current of 0.5 amperes flows through it?
notes.choices:
A) 1 volt
B) 0.25 volts
C) 2.5 volts
D) 1.5 volts
notes.choicesExplained: B: 0.25 is current divided by resistance. C: 2.5 is the sum. D: 1.5 is the difference.
notes.explanation: E = I × R = 0.5 A × 2 ohms = 1 V.

notes.front: What is the voltage across a 10-ohm resistor if a current of 1 ampere flows through it?
notes.choices:
A) 1 volt
B) 10 volts
C) 11 volts
D) 9 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 1 is the current, not the voltage. C: 11 is the sum. D: 9 is the difference.
notes.explanation: E = I × R = 1 A × 10 ohms = 10 V.

notes.front: What is the voltage across a 10-ohm resistor if a current of 2 amperes flows through it?
notes.choices:
A) 8 volts
B) 0.2 volts
C) 12 volts
D) 20 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 8 is the difference. B: 0.2 is current divided by resistance. C: 12 is the sum.
notes.explanation: E = I × R = 2 A × 10 ohms = 20 V.

notes.front: In which type of circuit is the current always the same through all components?
notes.choices:
A) Series
B) Parallel
C) Resonant
D) Branch
notes.choicesExplained: B: in parallel, the voltage is the same, not the current. C: a resonant circuit is defined by its parts, an inductor and a capacitor, not by equal current. D: “branch” is not the circuit type with the same current everywhere.
notes.explanation: Components in series sit one after another in a single path, so the same current passes through each in turn; in parallel it is the voltage that is the same.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D13, T5D14, T6D11

notes.front: In which type of circuit is the voltage always the same across all components?
notes.choices:
A) Series
B) Parallel
C) Resonant
D) Branch
notes.choicesExplained: A: in series, the current is the same, not the voltage. C: a resonant circuit is defined by its parts, an inductor and a capacitor, not by equal voltage. D: “branch” is not the circuit type with the same voltage everywhere.
notes.explanation: Components in parallel are each connected across the same two points, so each has the same voltage across it; in series it is the current that is the same.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D14, T5D13, T6D11

notes.front: What is always the same in a series circuit, and what in a parallel circuit?
notes.back: Series: the same current through every component. Parallel: the same voltage across every component.
notes.explanation: The pool asks both directions; swap them and you pick the wrong answer.

image.alt: Two circuits. Left, series: a battery and three resistors in one loop, labelled “same current through every component”. Right, parallel: three resistors each connected across the same battery, labelled “same voltage across every component”.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D13 and T5D14

notes.front: In Ohm’s law, when do you multiply and when do you divide?
notes.back: Multiply to find voltage (E = I × R); divide voltage to find current (E / R) or resistance (E / I).
notes.explanation: To find E, multiply I × R; to find I or R, divide E by the other one.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5D01, T5D02, T5D03
